extracted.intended_audience: general readers and writers of humorous literary sketches
extracted.subtask_description: Creating short humorous vignettes that sketch stereotyped or exaggerated types (here, varieties of married couples), using dialogue, repetition, contrast, and ironic detail to produce satire and comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: THE LOVING COUPLE
rubrics_metrics.description: Portray a couple whose public demonstrations of affection are extravagant, continuous, and ludicrously sentimental—public kissing, theatrical fainting, and mutual pet-names are emphasised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show their affection in both private and public contexts (at home, pic-nics, water-parties). Use small incidents (tapping under the chin, slipping in a boat, feigned fainting) to escalate comic effect; contrast their high sentiment with mundane concerns (asking about bottled stout and sandwiches). Examples: Mr. and Mrs. Leaver's repeated terms of endearment, Mrs. Leaver's theatrical fainting, the husband's comic exhaustion during rowing, and the group's delighted commentary ('What a loving couple you are!').

rubrics_metrics.name: THE CONTRADICTORY COUPLE
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketch a married pair defined entirely by mutual contradiction—they contradict each other constantly, even over trivial matters, creating escalating quarrels and absurd logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rapid back-and-forth dialogue where each partner insists on being right and accuses the other of contradiction. Include petty, specific disputes (number of doors in a house, who was at a sofa) and escalate to performative gestures (stalking off to bed, feigned sleep). Demonstrate how children and friends are drawn into or exasperated by the contradiction. Example lines: repeated 'Do you mean to say...' exchanges, and the exchange about Jenkins/Morgan and 'six feet' for Mrs. Parsons.

rubrics_metrics.name: THE COUPLE WHO DOTE UPON THEIR CHILDREN
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterise parents whose identities and conversations revolve obsessively around their numerous children—they mark time by children's events and recount endless anecdotes about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise an exaggerated number of children and a 'mental almanack' of child-related anniversaries. Use hyperbole (children are either remarkably healthy or disastrously unwell) and the parents' inability to stop connecting every topic to their offspring. Include scenes where guests are cornered by detailed accounts, and chaotic domestic tableaux (children swarming the table, pudding scene) to show how social life is dominated by parental boasting and egotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: THE COOL COUPLE
rubrics_metrics.description: Present spouses emotionally distant from each other—apathetic at home, polite and well-bred in society, often pursuing separate interests and excusing absence as trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the weather-glass allegory (one in when the other is out) to set the tone. Show quiet, ironic exchanges and mutual recrimination that resolve into polite separations (one goes to the club, the other to a visit). Contrast private apathy with public civility: they are 'best-bred' in society but cold at home. Use small scenes (yawning husband, lady's languid replies, mutual accusations of selfishness) to illustrate the gulf.

rubrics_metrics.name: THE PLAUSIBLE COUPLE
rubrics_metrics.description: Depict a couple whose primary talent is pleasing the world by unctuous, flattering, and adaptable behaviour—ever ready with exaggerated praise and gentle 'criticism' disguised as candour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how they can find merits and virtues everywhere, flatter with faux-independence ('we never flatter—we speak our minds'), and perform mutual pet-names and public concord. Use table-talk where both partners loudly celebrate a third party (the Clickits) and immediately echo each other's praise, demonstrating social performance and insincerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pointed dialogue to reveal character
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ crisp, representative dialogue as the primary means of revealing each couple's comic traits and driving the humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let speech rhythms, interruptions, repeated phrases, and specific quoted exclamations (e.g., 'Is he dead? Is he dead?') carry the comic action. Short, sharply punctuated lines and counter-accusations expose personalities more effectively than exposition. Dickens repeatedly uses dialogue exchanges to show contradiction, affection, and insincerity—model scenes on these exchanges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration and hyperbole
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnify characteristic traits to absurd extremes (children as prodigies of health or illness; perpetual pet names; counting doors as if vital) to create ridicule and comic distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Push ordinary domestic details into the extreme (many children, spectacular fainting, 'twins' recurring in every anecdote) so that the reader recognises the stereotype and laughs at its excess. Use specific, improbable incidents (falling out of a window unhurt and becoming proud) to underline the absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and escalating repetition for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeat key phrases, questions, or actions to build rhythm and intensify humour (e.g., persistent 'Is he dead?'; repeated mutual pet-terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ successive iterations of a line or gesture with small variations or increasing absurdity to heighten satire. The text uses repeated questioning, reiterated pet-names, and recurring references (the twins, anniversaries) to create comic momentum and to emphasize obsession or affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast and juxtaposition between sentiment and the mundane
rubrics_metrics.description: Place lofty sentimental language or dramatic behaviour alongside trivial, everyday concerns to underline comic incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let grand expressions of love or alarm be immediately followed by commonplace preoccupations (after fainting, Mr. Leaver enquires about 'bottled stout and sandwiches'). Juxtaposing high feeling with petty appetite or social performance produces ironic humour.
